flashcards.question: How big is SOCIAL INNOVATION globally?
flashcards.answer:
• 7% of the global GDP
• 10 million enterprises globally
• 2 trillion (USD) in annual revenue
• 200 million jobs
flashcards.explanation: Four headline numbers from the lecture.

flashcards.question: What does social innovation AIM to do?
flashcards.answer:
• Do something good in/for society
• Change social practices and/or structures
• Contribute to urban and community development
• Reorganize work processes
• Instil technological innovations with cultural meaning and relevance
• Make changes in the area of social work
• Innovate by means of digital connectivity
flashcards.explanation: Seven aims of social innovation.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE PREVALENT NOTIONS of social innovation?
flashcards.answer:
1. GOVERNANCE mechanism — changing governance processes to improve PARTICIPATION; 'social experimentation' that revitalizes policy; must have measurable outcomes

2. MARKET-BASED mechanism — 'creative recombination of existing assets into new business models' to address pressing social problems; ECONOMIC value is a MEANS to the END of creating SOCIAL value; individual entrepreneur as social change agent

3. COLLABORATIVE mechanism — innovation benefits from NETWORKS, co-operation and CO-PRODUCTION; communities create local solutions using local experience, knowledge and values; innovation as a knowledge problem, not a political one
flashcards.explanation: Governance / market-based / collaborative.

flashcards.question: How does social innovation connect to TOURISM entrepreneurship?
flashcards.answer:
Contributing to an inclusive, resilient, just and sustainable tourism sector through:

• Local community involvement
• Green and blue economies
• Ecological and sustainable capital creation
• Tourism tech for good
• Tourism education
• Women empowerment
flashcards.explanation: Six areas where social innovation meets tourism.

flashcards.question: What is the SOCIAL-SPATIAL IMPACT of Airbnb?
flashcards.answer:
• Owners rent out entire apartments PERMANENTLY via short-term rental platforms
• INVESTORS replace local property owners; long-term tenants replaced by TOURISTS
• Residents sell and move out (buy-to-let pressure + daily disruptions)
• Residential areas convert into TOURIST DISTRICTS (central Berlin streets; Ibiza housing shortage blocks teachers/doctors)
• 78% of Airbnb landlords are FOREIGN INVESTORS and professional developers
• Only 1% of Airbnb supply is residents sharing their homes (Alfama, Lisbon)
flashcards.explanation: The 'sharing economy' model can harm local communities — hence regulations.

flashcards.question: What are the ECONOMIC characteristics of developing countries?
flashcards.answer:
• LOW per capita real income
• HIGH population growth rate/size
• Higher rates of UNDER-EMPLOYMENT
• Dependence on the PRIMARY sector and exports of primary commodities
• Increase in poverty
• Lack of industries → increase in foreign investment
• BUT faster GDP growth (e.g. 7.8% in South Asia in 2021)
flashcards.explanation: The economic context for entrepreneurship.

flashcards.question: What characterises ENTREPRENEURSHIP in developing countries?
flashcards.answer:
• Limited access to resources and capabilities
• Widespread lack of properly functioning institutions
• Least favorable infrastructure and entrepreneurship-education levels
• WEAK/less efficient formal institutions (capital, labor, product markets, regulation)
• OVERRELIANCE on INFORMAL institutions
• Culturally based beliefs affect entrepreneurial activity
• LESS intensive competition
• GROWING demand for new products and services
flashcards.explanation: Weak formal institutions → informal institutions take over.

flashcards.question: What is the 'MIXED PICTURE' of entrepreneurship in developing countries?
flashcards.answer:
POSITIVE: wealth creation, making a difference, HIGH entrepreneurial activity, influence of social/cultural norms, confidence in the ability to start a business.

BUT: 2% OR LESS of adults are ESTABLISHED Business Owners.
flashcards.explanation: Lots of starting, little surviving.

flashcards.question: Case: NGO-owned restaurant in Phnom Penh — what went wrong?
flashcards.answer:
NGOs become social enterprises (community-based tourism) to diversify income as donor funding declines.

Goal: train local youth and reintegrate them into the workforce.

RESULT (over one year): the NGO became so focused on GENERATING REVENUE that NOT A SINGLE TRAINEE was reintegrated; introduced fees excluded non-paying beneficiaries (Dahles et al., 2020).
flashcards.explanation: MISSION DRIFT — revenue goals displaced the social mission.

flashcards.question: Case: Grootbos Lodge (South Africa) — what is the lesson?
flashcards.answer:
Owner set up a NON-PROFIT FOUNDATION financed equally by lodge tourism income and third-party donations.

Twofold vision: training project for unemployed women (sustainable livelihoods) + local organic food supplied to the hospitality business.

LESSON: the enterprise REMAINED DEPENDENT on external funding AND external know-how/training capacity.
flashcards.explanation: Dependency risk in social enterprises.

flashcards.question: Case: Eco-pads in India — what are the 4 strategic responses to institutional complexity?
flashcards.answer:
A sanitary napkin enterprise in southern India succeeded despite social taboos. Cherrier et al. (2018) identify 4 strategies that foster social innovation:

1. APPROPRIATION
2. INTEGRATION
3. DIFFERENTIATION
4. WORKING-THROUGH

These enable reaching a broader range of stakeholders, internalizing contextual influences, and creating social, economic and environmental value.
flashcards.explanation: Strategies for navigating institutional complexity.

flashcards.question: Case: 'Mageires' the social restaurant — what are its key features?
flashcards.answer:
Thessaloniki, Greece: healthy, good-quality GREEK food at reasonable prices, sustainably, during the economic crisis. Free delivery to people with mobility problems.

• 60% OF PROFITS REINVESTED for community benefits → operates under a 'DOUBLE BOTTOM LINE' of economic AND social goals

Sigala (2019): 3 MARKET CAPABILITIES for generating social value:
1. NETWORK STRUCTURE (institutions, suppliers, nutritionist, Facebook community)
2. MARKET PRACTICES (exchange, normalized, representational)
3. MARKET PICTURES (workshops, eat-and-learn, dialogues)
flashcards.explanation: 60% reinvested + 3 market capabilities.

learn.title: Entrepreneurship in Developing Countries & Social Innovation
learn.content:
Social Innovation — the Scale

7% of global GDP · 10 million enterprises · $2 trillion annual revenue · 200 million jobs

Three Prevalent Notions

1. GOVERNANCE: social experimentation revitalizing policy; participation; measurable outcomes

2. MARKET-BASED: creative recombination of existing assets into new business models; economic value = means to the end of social value

3. COLLABORATIVE: networks, co-operation, co-production; local knowledge and values

Airbnb's Social-Spatial Impact

  • Investors replace local owners; tourists replace long-term tenants
  • Residential areas → tourist districts (Berlin, Ibiza)
  • 78% of landlords = foreign investors; only 1% residents sharing homes (Alfama, Lisbon) → growing regulations

Developing Countries — Context

Economy: low per-capita income, high population growth, under-employment, primary-sector dependence, poverty — but fast GDP growth (7.8% South Asia 2021)

Entrepreneurship: limited resources, weak formal institutions → overreliance on informal institutions, less competition, growing demand

Mixed picture: high entrepreneurial activity BUT ≤ 2% of adults are Established Business Owners

Case Studies

Phnom Penh NGO restaurant: mission drift — revenue focus, zero trainees reintegrated (Dahles et al., 2020)

Grootbos Lodge (South Africa): training women + organic food, but dependent on external funding and know-how

Eco-pads (India): 4 strategies vs institutional complexity — appropriation, integration, differentiation, working-through (Cherrier et al., 2018)

Mageires (Thessaloniki): 60% profits reinvested, double bottom line; 3 market capabilities — network structure, market practices, market pictures (Sigala, 2019)

flashcards.question: Which weeks make up the two midterm 'halves' that the final combines?
flashcards.answer:
1st midterm (Weeks 2–7): concepts & theories of entrepreneurship, the entrepreneur (traits & influences), creativity & business idea, innovation, financing the business, franchising, planning.

2nd midterm (Weeks 9–13): failure & entrepreneurial learning, entrepreneurship & the economy, tourism entrepreneurship, social entrepreneurship, measuring value, contemporary issues (gender/diversity/migration), developing countries & social innovation.
flashcards.explanation: Week 8 = 1st midterm; the final covers everything.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: Match the theorist to the idea — Cantillon, Smith, Say, Mises, Kirzner, Schumpeter, Marshall, Menger.
flashcards.answer:
CANTILLON (1755): risk-taker bearing uncertainty
SMITH: transforms demand into supply; profit = reward
SAY: innovator-middleman between scientist and worker; superintendence
MISES: speculator; born not made
KIRZNER: alertness; continual discovery
SCHUMPETER: new 'productive combinations' (5); engine of change
MARSHALL: risk-taker AND administrator; active vs passive entrepreneurs
MENGER: heterogeneous individuals; special kind of labour service
flashcards.explanation: The theorist line-up appears in both halves of the course.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: Critical numbers across the course.
flashcards.answer:
• 1755 — Cantillon coins 'entrepreneur'
• 5 — Schumpeter's productive combinations
• 7 — Drucker's sources of opportunity; 7 value-measurement dimensions
• 9 — Business Model Canvas blocks
• 4 — types of social entrepreneurs; 4 crowdfunding types; 4 knowledge/skill types
• 98% — startups starting without formal investment
• 95% — VC applications rejected; £2M+ VC investments vs £10k–250k angels
• 5× — franchisee more likely to succeed (10% vs 52% failure)
• ~90% — long-run startup failure; 70% fail in years 2–5
• 3:1 — men vs women in business ownership; 2.3% of VC to women
• 45% — Fortune 500 founded by migrants or their children
• 7% — social innovation's share of global GDP
flashcards.explanation: Numbers are the fastest exam points.

flashcards.question: Connect CREATIVITY → INNOVATION → ENTREPRENEURSHIP → ECONOMY in one chain.
flashcards.answer: CREATIVITY produces new ideas (no need required) → ideas that are useful AND valuable become OPPORTUNITIES (finding vs building) → INNOVATION takes them effectively and profitably to satisfied customers (Kanter) → the ENTREPRENEUR acts on the innovation, financing it (bootstrapping → crowdfunding → angels/VC) and planning it (BMC → feasibility → pitch deck → business plan) → at MACRO level this raises capital formation, employment, technological progress; at MICRO level it creates new entities, jobs, goods and niche markets.
flashcards.explanation: The whole course as one storyline.

flashcards.question: How do FAILURE and LEARNING connect to fear of failure across cultures?
flashcards.answer:
~90% of startups fail long-run (70% in years 2–5). Failure is a PROCESS (stages of decline), caused by exogenous and internal factors, with warning signs of INACTION and faulty action.

Fear of failure DISABLES learning, investment and opportunity recognition — but tolerance differs (Africa & Latin America higher; Asia/Europe lower) and society shifts to 'risk rather than sin'.

Positive view: knowledge spillovers; Edison's '1,000 steps'; the failure resume.
flashcards.explanation: Failure (W9) is the hinge between the two halves.

flashcards.question: Cross-topic: how does SOCIAL entrepreneurship scale from a community café to changing systems?
flashcards.answer:
TYPES (small → large): COMMUNITY (local problem) → NON-PROFIT (business-savvy, social good) → TRANSFORMATIONAL (fills gaps governments/businesses miss) → GLOBAL (changes social systems).

Measure the value on 7 DIMENSIONS (impact, sustainability, innovation, scalability, community involvement, partnerships, awareness/advocacy) — while avoiding mission drift (Phnom Penh NGO) and dependency (Grootbos).
flashcards.explanation: Combines W11 types, W11 measurement and W13 case lessons.

learn.title: Final Exam Practice — How to Use
learn.content:
What is this category?

A cross-topic practice set combining all course weeks — exactly how the final mixes them. Use it AFTER reviewing the two midterm halves.

The course in one map

FOUNDATIONS (W2): origins & theorists → typologies → traits & social influences
CREATING (W3–W4): idea → creativity → opportunity → innovation (Drucker's 7, journey)
BUILDING (W5–W7): bootstrapping/crowdfunding/angels/VC → franchising → planning tools
CONTEXT (W9–W13): failure & learning → economy & tourism → social entrepreneurship & value → gender/diversity/migration trends → developing countries & social innovation

Cross-topic favourites

  • Theorist line-up: Cantillon → Smith → Say → Mises → Kirzner → Schumpeter → Marshall → Menger
  • Finding vs building opportunities; growth vs fixed mindset
  • Kickstarter all-or-nothing; angels vs VCs (numbers!)
  • Franchisee = intrapreneur; resource scarcity vs agency theory
  • Planning order: idea → BMC → feasibility → pitch deck → business plan
  • Failure stats (90% / 70% / 1-in-5) + fear-of-failure consequences
  • 4 social-entrepreneur types + 7 value dimensions + case lessons (mission drift!)
